title: Guided Project: See Your Network Traffic with Wireshark
subtitle: Capture your own computer's traffic in Wireshark and read it: a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake, HTTP beside HTTPS, display filters, followed streams and statistics.
outcomes: Capture traffic safely and lawfully on your own computer, and find your way around Wireshark's panes
Write display filters that find exactly the packets you need
Read a DNS lookup and a TCP three-way handshake packet by packet
Compare HTTP and HTTPS on the wire, and follow a TCP stream
Summarise a capture with Wireshark's Protocol Hierarchy and Conversations statistics
prerequisites: Basic networking ideas (IP addresses, ports, TCP and UDP) help but aren't required. You need a Windows, macOS or Linux computer where you may install Wireshark (free from wireshark.org) and capture packets, on a network you own or have permission to monitor, such as your home network.
description: Wireshark lets you see exactly what your computer says to the network, packet by packet. In this guided project you'll capture your own computer's traffic, on a network you own or are allowed to monitor, and learn to read it. Three short lessons cover capturing responsibly, finding your way around Wireshark's panes, writing display filters, following TCP streams and reading Wireshark's statistics. Then, in one hands-on lab, you'll capture a DNS lookup, a TCP three-way handshake and the same web page fetched over HTTP and over HTTPS, and explain what each packet shows, including what someone else on the network could and couldn't see. Your instructor reviews your findings.

modules.title: Capture and read your own traffic
modules.summary: Learn to capture responsibly and filter well, then capture a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and the same page over HTTP and HTTPS, and explain what each packet shows.

lessons.title: Capturing safely, and Wireshark's main window
objectives: Explain when you may capture network traffic and how to treat what you capture
Start and stop a capture and read Wireshark's three main panes
key_points: Capture only on networks and devices you own or have explicit permission to monitor: captures can contain other people's private data, and capturing without permission can break the law and workplace rules.
Treat capture files as sensitive: they can hold addresses, names, cookies and unencrypted content. Don't share them, and delete them when you've finished.
On a switched or Wi-Fi network, your computer normally sees its own traffic plus broadcasts and some multicast, which is all this project needs.

Wireshark's packet list shows one line per packet (number, time, source, destination, protocol, length and an Info summary); the packet details pane shows each layer's header as a tree; the packet bytes pane shows the raw bytes in hexadecimal.

Capture filters, set before a capture in BPF syntax such as port 53, decide what's recorded; display filters, typed in the filter bar such as dns, only hide packets from view and can be changed at any time.

Captures are saved as .pcapng files. Wireshark colours the packet list by rules, by default light purple for TCP, light blue for UDP and light green for HTTP, which View > Coloring Rules lets you see and change.

steps.do: Install Wireshark from wireshark.org. On Windows, let the installer add Npcap; on macOS, also install ChmodBPF (it comes with Wireshark) so you can capture without administrator rights; on Linux, install it from your distribution and allow non-root capture (on Debian and Ubuntu, add yourself to the wireshark group and log in again).

Open Wireshark. The welcome screen lists interfaces, each with a sparkline of activity: choose the one your computer is using (Wi-Fi or Ethernet on Windows, en0 on most Macs, a name such as wlan0 or enp0s3 on Linux).
Start capturing: double-click the interface, or select it and start a capture.
steps.see: Packets start to fill the packet list.

steps.do: Open a web page or two in your browser, then stop the capture.
Click a packet in the packet list and look at the packet details below it.
steps.see: One line per layer: Frame, Ethernet II (or another link layer), Internet Protocol, then TCP or UDP, then the application protocol if there is one.

steps.do: Select a header in the packet details and expand it to see its fields.
Click a field, such as the Source Address in the Internet Protocol header.
steps.see: The packet bytes pane highlights the bytes it came from.

steps.do: Open Capture > Options to see where a capture filter would go. This project leaves it empty and filters the display instead.
Save the capture with File > Save As, as a .pcapng file, somewhere private.

lessons.title: Display filters
objectives: Write display filters by protocol, address, port and field value
Combine filters, and build them from packet fields
key_points: Display filters use protocol and field names: dns shows DNS packets, tcp.port == 443 traffic to or from port 443, ip.addr == 192.168.1.20 packets to or from that address, and http.request only HTTP requests.
Filters combine with && (and), || (or) and ! (not), with brackets where needed: dns || tcp.port == 80, or !(arp || dns).
Comparisons include == and != for equality, > and < for numbers, and contains for text, as in dns.qry.name contains "example".
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 finds the first packet of every TCP handshake, and tls.handshake.type == 1 finds TLS Client Hello messages.
The filter bar turns green for a valid filter and red for an invalid one. Right-clicking a field in the packet details and choosing Apply as Filter > Selected builds a filter from it.
A display filter only hides packets: every packet is still in the capture, and clearing the filter shows them all again.

walkthrough.title: Filter a capture down to what matters

steps.do: Start a capture, look a name up in a terminal, open a web page, then stop the capture.
Type dns in the filter bar and press Enter.
steps.see: Only DNS packets: Standard query and Standard query response in the Info column.

steps.do: Show your HTTPS traffic.
Find the start of every TCP connection.
steps.see: One packet per connection your computer opened, with [SYN] in the Info column.

steps.do: Find the names you looked up.
Hide what you don't need.
Type a mistake, such as tcp.prot == 443.
steps.see: The filter bar turns red: there's no field called tcp.prot.

steps.do: Build a filter from a packet: filter dns, select a response, expand Domain Name System, right-click the query name and choose Apply as Filter > Selected.
steps.see: The filter bar fills in for you, with a filter such as dns.qry.name == "example.com".

steps.do: Clear the filter with the X at the right-hand end of the filter bar.

lessons.title: Following streams and reading statistics
objectives: Follow a TCP stream to see a conversation the way the application saw it
Summarise a capture with Protocol Hierarchy, Conversations and Endpoints
key_points: Analyze > Follow > TCP Stream shows the data of one TCP connection in order, with the client's data in one colour (red by default) and the server's in another (blue), and applies a display filter such as tcp.stream eq 3 for that connection.
Wireshark numbers the TCP connections in a capture from 0 upwards, as tcp.stream, so following a stream is a quick way to isolate one connection.

For plain HTTP, a followed stream reads like text: the request line and headers, then the response's status line, headers and page. For HTTPS, everything after the TLS handshake is encrypted application data.

Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy shows each protocol's share of the packets and bytes; Statistics > Conversations lists the traffic between each pair of addresses or ports; Statistics > Endpoints lists each address with its packets and bytes.
Statistics > Capture File Properties shows when a capture started and ended, how many packets it holds and which interface it used, and Statistics > I/O Graphs plots traffic over time.
Closing the Follow window with Back restores the filter you had before; Close leaves the stream's filter in place.

walkthrough.title: Follow a stream and summarise a capture

steps.do: In a capture with some web traffic, filter for tcp and select any packet of a connection.
Open the Follow window for that connection: right-click the packet and choose Follow > TCP Stream, or use Analyze > Follow > TCP Stream.
steps.see: The connection's data, the client's in red and the server's in blue; for HTTPS, mostly unreadable encrypted bytes.

steps.do: Look at the bottom of the window: the stream's number, and a choice between the entire conversation and each direction on its own.
Click Close and look at the filter bar.
steps.see: tcp.stream eq followed by the stream's number.

steps.do: Clear the filter, so the statistics count every packet, and open Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy.
steps.see: A tree starting at Frame, with lines such as Internet Protocol Version 4, Transmission Control Protocol, User Datagram Protocol and the protocols inside them, each with its percentage of packets and bytes.

steps.do: Open Statistics > Conversations and choose the TCP tab.
steps.see: One row per TCP connection: Address A, Port A, Address B, Port B, then packets, bytes and duration.

steps.do: Sort by Bytes to find the biggest conversation, then right-click it and use Apply as Filter to show only its packets.
Open Statistics > Capture File Properties.
steps.see: The capture's start and end, its length, its number of packets and the interface it used.

lab.title: Capture and explain your own traffic
lab.goal: Capture your own computer's traffic while you look up a name and fetch the same page over HTTP and over HTTPS, then use filters, Follow TCP Stream and statistics to explain each step, and what someone else on the network could see.
setup: Wireshark installed with permission to capture: Npcap on Windows, ChmodBPF on macOS, or membership of the wireshark group on Linux
A computer on a network you own or have permission to monitor, such as your home network
curl, which comes with Windows 10 and 11, macOS and most Linux systems
Other programs that use the network closed, so the capture is easier to read

steps.do: Start a capture on your active interface.
In a terminal, look up the name example.com.
Fetch the page over plain HTTP. On Windows, type curl.exe, so that PowerShell doesn't run a different command of its own.
steps.see: The page's HTML, including <title>Example Domain</title>.

steps.do: Fetch the same page over HTTPS.
Stop the capture, and save it privately as my-traffic.pcapng.
DNS: filter dns, find your query and its response, and expand Domain Name System in the response.
steps.see: Standard query followed by an ID and A example.com, then Standard query response with the same ID; under Answers, the name, type A, a TTL and an address. You may also see AAAA queries, for IPv6 addresses.

steps.do: In the same response, expand User Datagram Protocol and note the ports.
steps.see: Source Port 53 (the DNS server) and a high destination port on your computer.

steps.do: Handshake: filter the HTTP connection and look at its first three packets.
steps.see: [SYN] from your computer, [SYN, ACK] from the server, then [ACK] from your computer: Seq=0, then Seq=0 Ack=1, then Seq=1 Ack=1, in relative sequence numbers.

steps.do: HTTP: filter http and find the request and the response.
steps.see: GET / HTTP/1.1 from your computer, and HTTP/1.1 200 OK (text/html) from the server.

steps.do: Right-click the GET request and choose Follow > TCP Stream. Read the request (red) and the response (blue), then click Close and note the filter it leaves.
steps.see: GET / HTTP/1.1, Host: example.com and a User-Agent naming curl, then HTTP/1.1 200 OK, the headers and the page's HTML; the filter bar shows tcp.stream eq and the stream's number.

steps.do: HTTPS: find the Client Hello and expand Transport Layer Security down to the server_name extension.
steps.see: Server Name: example.com: the name is visible, though everything after the handshake will be encrypted.

steps.do: Follow that TLS connection's TCP stream and compare it with the HTTP one, then look at its packets in the list.
steps.see: Unreadable bytes after the handshake, and packets described as Application Data.

steps.do: Clear the filter, open Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy and copy it with its Copy button (as CSV).
Open Statistics > Conversations, choose the TCP tab and copy it the same way.
Write your explanation: for DNS, the handshake, HTTP and HTTPS, which packets you found, what they show, and what someone else watching the network could learn from each.

checks.text: The DNS query and response for example.com are shown, carried over UDP port 53.
The HTTP connection's three-way handshake is shown in order.
The HTTP request and response are found, and the followed stream is readable.
The TLS Client Hello shows the server's name, and the HTTPS connection is unreadable after the handshake.
The display filter left by Follow TCP Stream is given.
The Protocol Hierarchy and the TCP conversations are summarised.
The explanation says what an observer could see for HTTP (the whole request and page) compared with HTTPS (the addresses and server name, but not the content).

lab.submit: Paste a few packet-list lines for each part (select them, right-click and choose Copy, then Summary as Text), the HTTP stream from the Follow window, the Server Name line from the Client Hello, the stream filter, your copied Protocol Hierarchy and TCP conversations, and your explanation. Don't attach the capture file.
hints: No interfaces listed? On Windows, reinstall Wireshark with Npcap; on macOS, run the ChmodBPF installer; on Linux, check you're in the wireshark group and log in again.
No DNS packets for example.com? Your computer may have cached the answer: run ipconfig /flushdns on Windows, or ask a public resolver directly with nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8.
No HTTP packets? Make sure you used curl with http://, not a browser, which may switch to HTTPS by itself.
Too much unrelated traffic? Find the server's address in the DNS response and filter with ip.addr == followed by that address.
